The Superb lyrebird (Menura novaehollandiae) undertakes an extraordinary investment in its single-egg clutch, a life-history strategy that yields a maximum reproductive rate of one egg per clutch [N_R_i = one egg per clutch]. Under the thermal conditions typical of the breeding season in its temperate forest habitat (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), females are capable of producing only one brood each year [F_R_i = one brood each year], a remarkably low annual fecundity compared to other passeriforms of similar body size. This constraint is partially offset by significant parental care, with the single altricial nestling receiving both brooding and provisioning almost exclusively from the female, as the male contributes little beyond courtship display during the early breeding period. Eggs incubated at a mean temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] require a long developmental period of 50 days [ab = 50 days] until hatching, a duration that reflects the energetic demands of producing a well-developed, semi-precocial chick in a cool, wet forest environment. The slow embryonic growth rate is likely an adaptation to unpredictable food resources during the austral spring.

Neonatal body mass at hatching is a modest 41 grams [Wwb = 41 grams], a value representing only a fraction of the eventual adult mass and highlighting the altricial strategy of this species despite its large ultimate size. This initial wet weight is measured soon after emergence from the egg, before the chick has taken its first meal from the female. Growth during the nestling period is rapid, and the chicks are brooded continuously for the first several weeks to maintain thermal stability. The high metabolic demands of feather production and skeletal maturation necessitate a steady delivery of invertebrate prey by the attending parent. Males and females diverge substantially in their adult body mass, a manifestation of strong sexual size dimorphism that is among the most extreme recorded in any passerine bird. The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult females reaches approximately 680.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 680.2 grams], while their male counterparts far exceed this at maturity.

The disparity in mass between the sexes is even more pronounced: adult males attain an asymptotic body mass of 1099.7 grams [Wwi = 1099.7 grams], nearly double that of females, a divergence that ranks among the most pronounced within the Passeriformes. This marked dimorphism is closely linked to the species' elaborate lek-mating system, where larger males with more developed tail plumes achieve higher mating success through competitive displays. The substantial somatic investment required to reach this large body size delays the onset of reproductive maturity. Field studies indicate that males attain puberty at approximately 141 days after hatching [tp = approximately 141 days after hatching], although functional maturity and successful territory acquisition may be deferred for several ad at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]ditional years. Females, by contrast, mature somewhat faster in terms of gonadal development but still delay first breeding until they can secure a suitable nest site away from predators. The time since birth at first brood for females is estimated at 6.5 years [tR = 6.5 years] under the warm conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

Fledging occurs after a protracted nestling period of 47 days since birth [tx = 47 days since birth] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], during which the developing chick progresses from a downy hatchling to a fully feathered juvenile capable of short flights. This extended dependency is unusual among passerines and reflects the challenges of foraging in dense leaf litter, where young birds require time to learn complex prey-handling techniques. After leaving the nest, the fledgling remains in its mother's territory for several more months, gradually refining its foraging skills before dispersal. The initial wet weight of the egg at laying averages 61.5 grams [Ww0 = 61.5 grams], representing a substantial energetic investment for the female given her own body mass and the single-egg clutch. Egg composition is dominated by yolk and albumen, providing the necessary nutrients for the 50-day incubation period.

Maximum recorded longevity for the species has been documented at 17.9 years [am = 17.9 years] under the thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], characteristic of its montane habitat. This extended life span is consistent with a slow life-history strategy characterized by low annual fecundity, deferred reproduction, and high adult survival. Older males often dominate display sites and sire the majority of offspring in a given season, underscoring the selective advantage of longevity in this lekking species. The seasonal timing of reproductive events is tightly coupled with invertebrate prey abundance, which peaks during the austral spring and early summer. Predation pressure from raptors and mammalian carnivores necessitates vigilant nest-site selection, typically in sheltered gullies with dense understory vegetation. The complex vocal mimicry for which the species is famous likely serves dual functions in mate attraction and territorial defense, requiring years of practice to perfect.
